description: Reframes RS-041 from the Vienna-Convention blue crossing panel onto W306, the real SA sign. RS-041 was WITHDRAWN on 2026-07-30 (data-repairs-2026-07-30.json) for describing a blue rectangular sign with a pedestrian on zebra stripes as South African — that sign is European; SA has no blue panel marking a crossing. It has sat at review_status='draft' ever since, which is how a withdrawal is recorded here. The sign it described was withdrawn a day later (withdraw-foreign-signs-2026-07-31.json, R360 / R360-LES). This op does NOT restore the old claim: the prompt, answer and explanation are rewritten onto W306, whose meaning is read verbatim from Schedule 1. The three distractors were already good — two of them describe real SA signs — so they survive with the answer moved. Decision: John, 2026-08-03, after the sign hunt in K53-39/K53-40 established there is no blue SA crossing sign. Stays 'draft' deliberately: the content is now correct, but constraint 9 needs a named human to approve, and the admin editor still cannot record one.

set.prompt: A triangular sign with a red border, showing a pedestrian on zebra stripes, means:
options: Pedestrians are prohibited on this stretch of road
You are at the crossing now — give way to anyone already on it
A marked pedestrian crossing is ahead
set.explanation: A red triangle warns of something ahead — the crossing is still in front of you, so slow down and be ready to stop. The crossing itself carries no sign panel; it is the painted lines on the road. Give way to anyone already on it when you get there.
set.source_citation: NRTR 2000 Sch 1 — W306 pedestrian crossing sign; reg 315(2) (pedestrian's right of way in a pedestrian crossing)

ops.why: The explanation was first written in verification register — it quoted Schedule 1 by name and used 'your half of the roadway'. That is the citation's job, and source_citation already carries it; the learner-facing text should teach the contrast instead. Rewritten to the house voice measured across the 71 approved signs items (median 187 chars, opens plainly, names the confusion): the confusion this question turns on is AHEAD versus AT IT, so that leads. No sign code in the prose either — sign_code renders the artwork, so the learner is already looking at it. Deliberately NOT mentioning that Europe has a blue crossing panel: that misconception came from our own withdrawn question, not from SA learners, and naming a foreign sign would plant it. sign_code and objective_code are DIFFERENT columns doing different jobs — sign_code picks the artwork the quiz renders from /signs/<code>.svg, objective_code links the item to a learning objective — and both were R5. The first pass of this repair moved only objective_code, leaving the question asking about a red triangle while the quiz would have rendered the R5 red diamond. A sweep of all 27 questions carrying a sign_code found RS-041 the only row where the two diverged, so this is a one-off, not a class. Old prompt: 'A blue rectangular sign showing a pedestrian on zebra stripes means:' with the answer 'This is a pedestrian crossing — give way to pedestrians on it' and an explanation calling it 'the blue command sign'. Every part of that is the Vienna Convention sign used in Europe. Schedule 1 to the National Road Traffic Regulations describes W306 — Triangle: red retro-reflective, Symbol: black semi-matt, Background: white retro-reflective — as 'Warns a road user of a marked pedestrian crossing ahead'. Note 'marked': the crossing itself is the RTM3/RTM4 road markings, which is why no panel marks it. objective_code moves R5 -> W306; R5 was wrong twice over, being the red-diamond 'Pedestrian priority sign' rather than anything blue or rectangular. The yielding duty in the explanation is reg 315(2): the driver 'shall yield the right of way, slowing down or stopping if need be' to a pedestrian within the crossing who is on the driver's half of the roadway, or approaching so closely from the opposite half as to be in danger. Distractor 1 now describes R218 (pedestrian prohibited) and distractor 2 the mistake the sign is most often confused with, so both stay honest wrong answers.
